title: Air Cargo Dangerous Goods Basics
description: Practise spotting dangerous goods, reading labels, and making decisions from check-in to the cargo hold.

modules.title: Recognising dangerous goods
modules.summary: Meet the nine hazard classes and spot clues hiding in everyday cargo descriptions.

lessons.title: Meet the nine hazard classes
lessons.body: Hazard classes describe the kinds of risks materials can present in transport. Use these examples to recognise possible dangerous goods. Actual classification depends on the specific product and its properties.
lessons.funFact: Your whipped cream might deserve a second look. Some whipped cream dispensers are aerosols, which belong in the gases class.

groups.heading: 3. Flammable liquids
groups.examples: Some paints, paint thinners, and perfumes.

groups.heading: 4. Flammable solids and related hazards
groups.examples: Strike-anywhere matches. This class also includes substances liable to spontaneous combustion and substances that release flammable gas when wet.

groups.heading: 5. Oxidizers and organic peroxides
groups.examples: Some concentrated hydrogen peroxide products and some curing products.

groups.heading: 6. Toxic and infectious substances
groups.examples: Some pesticides and certain infectious substances.

groups.heading: 7. Radioactive material
groups.examples: Certain materials used in nuclear medicine.

groups.heading: 8. Corrosive substances
groups.examples: Some acids and wet-cell battery electrolyte.

lessons.title: The mystery event supplies
lessons.intro: A carton described as “event supplies” arrives at the desk. The sender mentions that it includes spray paint cans. What does that detail tell you?

nodes.text: The description says “event supplies,” but the sender confirms the spray paint is in aerosol cans.

choices.label: Flag the aerosol for review by the person responsible for dangerous goods.
choices.feedback: Good catch. The party banner can wait. An aerosol is a clue that the contents may be regulated as dangerous goods.

choices.label: Treat the carton as ordinary cargo because the description only says “event supplies.”
choices.feedback: That description is too broad. The confirmed aerosol matters when identifying possible dangerous goods.

nodes.text: The reviewer asks why you flagged the carton. What do you include in your handoff?

choices.label: Share the original description and the sender's confirmation that it includes aerosol spray paint.
choices.feedback: That gives the reviewer something useful to work with. The confirmed product detail explains why you flagged the carton.

choices.label: Repeat “event supplies” and leave the product detail out.
choices.feedback: The reviewer still needs to know what raised your concern. Include the specific detail the sender confirmed.

nodes.text: The reviewer has the original description and the confirmed product detail.

outcome.summary: You spotted the clue and made a clear handoff.
outcome.whatWentRight: You flagged the carton and passed along the specific clue that prompted the review.
outcome.whatToReview: Recognising a clue comes before confirming the product's classification.

nodes.text: The reviewer has to ask what the carton contains.

outcome.summary: The flag got through. The important detail stayed at the desk.
outcome.whatWentRight: You spotted the aerosol and flagged the carton for review.
outcome.whatToReview: When you hand off a case, include the product detail that made you flag it.

nodes.text: The description hides a clue you already had.

outcome.summary: The carton escaped review in this scenario.
outcome.whatWentRight: You noticed the description used on the carton.
outcome.whatToReview: A broad description can contain many kinds of products. Pay attention to specific clues such as an aerosol can.

lessons.title: Sort the samples
lessons.prompt: Match the named examples to the hazard classes from the earlier lesson.
lessons.hintText: Match each item to its clue: gas under pressure, a flammable liquid, or dry ice. The field guide lists an example for each.

questions.prompt: How many hazard classes are used to describe transport risks?
questions.explanation: There are nine main hazard classes. Some are split further into divisions.

questions.prompt: Which hazard class includes aerosol spray paint?
questions.explanation: Aerosols are listed under gases because they contain gas under pressure.

questions.prompt: Which hazard class includes dry ice?
options: Class 4 · Flammable solids and related hazards
questions.explanation: Dry ice is a Class 9 example.

questions.prompt: Which description gives you the strongest reason to ask about batteries?
questions.explanation: Rechargeable electronics can contain lithium batteries. Confirm the actual contents before relying on a cargo description.

modules.title: Reading labels and markings
modules.summary: Recognise hazard labels, identification numbers, and orientation markings.

lessons.title: Three clues on one carton
lessons.body: A package can carry several kinds of information at the same time. Read each one and compare it with the shipment details. These illustrations are simplified practice examples.
lessons.funFact: A single package can have a label for its primary hazard and another for a subsidiary hazard.

groups.heading: Hazard label
groups.examples: A diamond-shaped label communicates a hazard. For example, a Class 3 label identifies a flammable-liquid hazard.

groups.heading: UN identification number
groups.examples: A number such as UN1263 identifies a dangerous-goods entry. Check it against the shipment information.

groups.heading: Orientation arrows
groups.examples: When these arrows are present, they show which way is up.

lessons.title: The two numbers
lessons.intro: A carton and its paperwork reach the desk at the same time.

nodes.text: The UN identification number on the carton differs from the number on the paperwork.

choices.label: Pause the shipment review and refer the mismatch for verification.
choices.feedback: Good catch. Flag the two values so a trained reviewer can resolve the discrepancy.

choices.label: Treat the paperwork as correct and move on.
choices.feedback: The package marking still conflicts with the paperwork. One value alone cannot resolve the discrepancy.

nodes.text: The two values are recorded for the reviewer.

outcome.summary: The mismatch was caught before the carton moved on.
outcome.whatWentRight: You compared the marking and the paperwork instead of trusting one source.
outcome.whatToReview: A hazard label and a UN number communicate different things.

nodes.text: The unresolved mismatch reaches the next desk.

outcome.summary: The paperwork check missed a conflict.
outcome.whatWentRight: You read one of the identifiers.
outcome.whatToReview: Compare both values and flag any difference.

lessons.title: Match the package clues
lessons.prompt: Put each clue in the bin that describes what it communicates.
lessons.hintText: Read the different jobs the symbols do: warn, identify, or show which way is up.

questions.prompt: What do two upward orientation arrows indicate?
questions.explanation: Orientation arrows indicate the upright position.

questions.prompt: What does a hazard label communicate?
questions.explanation: A hazard label communicates a primary or subsidiary hazard.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of a UN identification number marking?
questions.explanation: A UN identification number begins with UN followed by four digits.

questions.prompt: What should happen when an identifier and the paperwork disagree in this training scenario?
questions.explanation: An unresolved conflict needs review before a decision is made.

modules.title: Acceptance and packing checks
modules.summary: Practise identifying questions and discrepancies at a cargo desk.

lessons.title: At the acceptance desk
lessons.body: A check-in decision brings several pieces of information together. Use the approved checks for the shipment and your role, and refer unresolved questions to an authorised reviewer.
lessons.funFact: Packaging suitability depends on what’s inside and on the transport conditions, even when two boxes look alike.

groups.heading: Check the information
groups.examples: Compare the shipment details with the visible markings and labels.

groups.heading: Observe package condition
groups.examples: Visible damage or a compromised closure can be a reason to pause and escalate.

groups.heading: Use the authorised process
groups.examples: Give the reviewer the specific discrepancy and keep the shipment decision pending until it is resolved.

lessons.title: The dented carton
lessons.intro: You’re taking over the desk at a busy time. The next carton is described as dangerous goods.

nodes.text: The paperwork looks consistent, but the carton has a crushed corner and an open seam.

choices.label: Pause and describe the visible damage to the authorised reviewer.
choices.feedback: The paperwork is one part of the check. The open seam is a separate concern.

choices.label: Approve it because the paperwork matches the labels.
choices.feedback: Matching paperwork leaves the condition question unresolved.

nodes.text: The package is referred for a condition assessment.

outcome.summary: You caught a problem the paperwork could not show.
outcome.whatWentRight: You separated package condition from documentation.
outcome.whatToReview: Use the approved process when there is an unresolved concern.

nodes.text: The shipment decision was made without resolving the damage.

outcome.whatWentRight: You compared the paperwork with the label.
outcome.whatToReview: Look at package condition as its own part of the review.

lessons.title: Sort the desk notes
lessons.prompt: Match each observation to the part of the check it belongs to.

items.label: A visible split in the seam
A blank field on the shipment paperwork

lessons.hintText: Ask where you found the issue: on the paperwork, on a label, or on the physical package.

questions.prompt: Which observation is about the package’s physical condition?
questions.explanation: An open seam is visible damage to the package itself.

questions.prompt: A dispatch deadline is approaching and a discrepancy remains. What is the sound decision?
options: Rely on the deadline as the decision rule
questions.explanation: A deadline doesn’t resolve a discrepancy. Use the approved review process.

questions.prompt: What helps determine whether packaging is suitable?
options: The package’s position in the queue
The hazard classification and physical properties of the contents
questions.explanation: Packaging selection depends on the material and the applicable conditions for transport.

questions.prompt: Which handoff is most useful to a reviewer?
options: The outer carton has an open seam on the lower edge
questions.explanation: A specific observation is easier for the reviewer to assess.

modules.title: Emergencies and spills
modules.summary: Work through decisions in simulated cargo incidents.

lessons.title: An unknown leak
lessons.intro: You are a cargo-desk worker in a simulated facility with a site emergency plan.

nodes.text: You notice liquid where a parcel was placed, and you do not know what it is.

choices.label: Move away and report the observation promptly through the site emergency procedure.
choices.feedback: Good call. Report what you saw and where you saw it, from a safe place.

choices.label: Wait for someone else to notice it.
choices.feedback: Waiting delays the report and leaves others unaware of the concern.

nodes.text: The designated responders receive the report.

outcome.summary: You raised the alert while the substance remained unidentified.
outcome.whatWentRight: You shared an observable fact and its location.
outcome.whatToReview: Know the reporting procedure for your site and role.

nodes.text: The concern was left unreported during the shift.

outcome.whatToReview: Report a suspected incident promptly through the site procedure.

lessons.title: Smoke near the cargo area
lessons.intro: You’re in a ground cargo facility in this simulation.

nodes.text: You see smoke near a cargo staging bay. Your site plan describes how to report emergencies and evacuate.

choices.label: Follow the site alert and evacuation procedure and give the location when safe.
choices.feedback: A clear location helps the response team act. Follow the evacuation instructions for your site.

choices.label: Wait nearby for a more obvious sign before reporting.
choices.feedback: Smoke is enough to raise a concern. Waiting delays the emergency alert.

nodes.text: The designated team receives the location and staff follow the plan.

outcome.summary: Your report helped the site response get started.
outcome.whatWentRight: You raised the alert and followed the site plan.
outcome.whatToReview: Know the alarm and evacuation procedure before an emergency.

nodes.text: The alert was delayed while staff waited for more information.

outcome.summary: The response team learned about the concern later.
outcome.whatToReview: Report what you can observe and follow the emergency plan.

lessons.title: Damage before handoff
lessons.intro: A colleague spots damage on a dangerous-goods package during a simulated handoff.

nodes.text: A side of the carton is torn. The handoff record has already been prepared.

choices.label: Keep the handoff pending and report the visible damage through the site procedure.
choices.feedback: The prepared record does not settle the new condition issue. Share what changed.

choices.label: Proceed because the earlier record is already complete.
choices.feedback: The earlier record does not reflect what you can see now.

nodes.text: The damage is logged and the handoff remains pending review.

outcome.summary: You brought new information into the decision.
outcome.whatWentRight: You recognised that package condition had changed since the paperwork was prepared.
outcome.whatToReview: Follow the site’s response process if the situation changes or an immediate hazard is suspected.

nodes.text: The handoff remained dependent on outdated information.

outcome.summary: New damage was missed in the handoff decision.
outcome.whatWentRight: You checked that there was a record.
outcome.whatToReview: Report newly visible damage through the site procedure before proceeding.

questions.prompt: Which is the clearest first report from a safe place?
options: I saw liquid beside a carton at bay 4; the substance is unknown
questions.explanation: Describe observable facts and the location. Leave unconfirmed details open.

questions.prompt: What guides your actions in a workplace emergency?
options: Your site’s emergency plan and your assigned role
The last entry on the manifest
questions.explanation: Emergency plans define how to report, alert, and evacuate at a site.

questions.prompt: You notice smoke in a staging bay. What matters first in this scenario?
options: Waiting for someone to identify the package
Promptly following the site’s emergency alert and evacuation procedure
questions.explanation: Raise the alert and follow the plan for the location.

questions.prompt: New visible damage appears after paperwork was prepared. What has changed?
options: The actual condition of the package
The previous record has been automatically updated
questions.explanation: The new observation matters even though the paperwork already exists.
